{{Short description|Numbers whose differences are not squares}}
{{good article}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''square-difference-free set''' is a [[set (mathematics)|set]] of [[natural number]]s, no two of which differ by a [[square number]]. [[Hillel Furstenberg]] and [[András Sárközy]] [[mathematical proof|proved]] in the late 1970s the '''Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem''' of [[additive number theory]] showing that, in a certain sense, these sets cannot be very large. In the game of [[subtract a square]], the positions where the next player loses form a square-difference-free set. Another square-difference-free set is obtained by doubling the [[Moser–de Bruijn sequence]].

The best known [[upper bound]] on the size of a square-difference-free set of numbers up to <math>n</math> is only slightly sublinear, but the largest known sets of this form are significantly smaller, of size <math>\approx n^{0.733412}</math>. Closing the gap between these upper and lower bounds remains an [[open problem]]. The sublinear size bounds on square-difference-free sets can be generalized to sets where certain other [[polynomial]]s are forbidden as differences between pairs of elements.

==Example==
An example of a set with no square differences arises in the game of [[subtract a square]], invented by [[Richard Arnold Epstein|Richard A. Epstein]] and first described in 1966 by [[Solomon W. Golomb]]. In this game, two players take turns removing coins from a pile of coins; the player who removes the last coin wins. In each turn, the player can only remove a nonzero square number of coins from the pile.<ref name="golomb">{{citation
 | last = Golomb | first = Solomon W. | authorlink = Solomon W. Golomb
 | doi = 10.1016/S0021-9800(66)80016-9
 | journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]]
 | mr = 0209015
 | pages = 443–458
 | title = A mathematical investigation of games of "take-away"
 | volume = 1
 | issue = 4 | year = 1966| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> Any position in this game can be described by an [[integer]], its number of coins.
The non-negative integers can be partitioned into "cold" positions, in which the player who is about to move is losing, and "hot" positions, in which the player who is about to move can win by moving to a cold position. No two cold positions can differ by a square, because if they did then a player faced with the larger of the two positions could move to the smaller position and win. Thus, the cold positions form a set with no square difference:
{{block indent|left=1.6|0, 2, 5, 7, 10, 12, 15, 17, 20, 22, 34, 39, 44, … {{OEIS|id=A030193}}}}
These positions can be generated by a [[greedy algorithm]] in which the cold positions are generated in numerical order, at each step selecting the smallest number that does not have a square difference with any previously selected {{nowrap|number.<ref name="golomb"/><ref>{{Cite OEIS|A030193|mode=cs2}}</ref>}} As Golomb observed, the cold positions are infinite, and more strongly the number of cold positions up to <math>n</math> is at least proportional {{nowrap|to <math>\sqrt n</math>.}} For, if there were fewer cold positions, there wouldn't be enough of them to supply a winning move to each hot position.<ref name="golomb"/>
The Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem shows, however, that the cold positions are less frequent than hot positions: for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math>, and for all large {{nowrap|enough <math>n</math>,}} the proportion of cold positions up to <math>n</math> is {{nowrap|at most <math>\varepsilon</math>.}} That is, when faced with a starting position in the range from {{nowrap|1 to <math>n</math>,}} the first player can win from most of these positions.<ref>The applicability of this theorem to the sequence produced by the greedy algorithm is implicit in {{harvtxt|Ruzsa|1984}}, who begins his paper with the statement that, "obviously", the greedy sequence must have size at least proportional to the square root. {{harvtxt|Lyall|Rice|2015}} state that a construction of {{harvtxt|Ruzsa|1984}} generates sets "much larger than the set yielded by the greedy algorithm", but do not provide bounds or citations that detail the size of the greedy set.</ref>
Numerical evidence suggests that the actual number of cold positions {{nowrap|up to <math>n</math>}} is {{nowrap|approximately <math>n^{0.7}</math>.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Eppstein | first = David | authorlink = David Eppstein
 | editor1-last = Ito | editor1-first = Hiro
 | editor2-last = Leonardi | editor2-first = Stefano
 | editor3-last = Pagli | editor3-first = Linda | editor3-link = Linda Pagli
 | editor4-last = Prencipe | editor4-first = Giuseppe
 | arxiv = 1804.06515
 | contribution = Faster evaluation of subtraction games
 | doi = 10.4230/LIPIcs.FUN.2018.20
 | pages = 20:1–20:12
 | publisher = Schloss Dagstuhl
 | series = Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics (LIPIcs)
 | title = Proc. 9th Int. Conf. Fun with Algorithms (FUN 2018)
 | volume = 100
 | year = 2018| doi-access = free | isbn = 9783959770675 | s2cid = 4952124 }}</ref>}}

==Upper bounds==
According to the Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem, if <math>S</math> is a square-difference-free set, then the [[natural density]] of <math>S</math> is zero. That is, for every <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, and for all sufficiently large <math>n</math>, the fraction of the numbers up to <math>n</math> that are in <math>S</math> is less than <math>\varepsilon</math>. Equivalently, every set of natural numbers with positive [[upper density]] contains two numbers whose difference is a square, and more strongly contains infinitely many such pairs.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Eisner | first1 = Tanja | author1-link = Tanja Eisner
 | last2 = Farkas | first2 = Bálint
 | last3 = Haase | first3 = Markus
 | last4 = Nagel | first4 = Rainer
 | contribution = 20.5 The Furstenberg–Sárközy Theorem
 | contribution-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=ZWj_CgAAQBAJ&pg=PA455
 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-16898-2
 | isbn = 978-3-319-16897-5
 | location = Cham, Switzerland
 | mr = 3410920
 | pages = 455–457
 | publisher = Springer
 | series = [[Graduate Texts in Mathematics]]
 | title = Operator Theoretic Aspects of Ergodic Theory
 | volume = 272
 | year = 2015}}.</ref> The Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem was [[conjecture]]d by [[László Lovász]], and proved independently in the late 1970s by [[Hillel Furstenberg]] and [[András Sárközy]], after whom it is named.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Furstenberg | first = Harry | authorlink = Hillel Furstenberg
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02813304 | doi-access=
 | journal = [[Journal d'Analyse Mathématique]]
 | mr = 0498471
 | pages = 204–256
 | title = Ergodic behavior of diagonal measures and a theorem of Szemerédi on arithmetic progressions
 | volume = 31
 | year = 1977| s2cid = 120917478 }}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Sárkőzy | first = A. | authorlink = András Sárközy
 | doi = 10.1007/BF01896079 | doi-access=free
 | issue = 1–2
 | journal = [[Acta Mathematica Hungarica|Acta Mathematica Academiae Scientiarum Hungaricae]]
 | mr = 0466059
 | pages = 125–149
 | title = On difference sets of sequences of integers. I
 | url = https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1978-19a.pdf
 | volume = 31
 | year = 1978| s2cid = 122018775 }}.</ref> Since their work, several other proofs of the same result have been published, generally either simplifying the previous proofs or strengthening the bounds on how sparse a square-difference-free set must be.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Green | first = Ben | authorlink = Ben Green (mathematician)
 | doi = 10.1215/S0012-7094-02-11422-7
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Duke Mathematical Journal]]
 | mr = 1920188
 | pages = 215–238
 | title = On arithmetic structures in dense sets of integers
 | volume = 114
 | year = 2002| url = http://www.dspace.cam.ac.uk/handle/1810/237036 | url-access = subscription
 }}.</ref><ref name="l13">{{citation
 | last = Lyall | first = Neil
 | arxiv = 1107.0243
 | doi = 10.1090/S0002-9939-2013-11628-X | doi-access=free
 | issue = 7
 | journal = [[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]]
 | mr = 3043007
 | pages = 2253–2264
 | title = A new proof of Sárközy's theorem
 | volume = 141
 | year = 2013| s2cid = 16842750
 }}.</ref><ref name="tao">{{citation|url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2013/02/28/a-fourier-free-proof-of-the-furstenberg-sarkozy-theorem/|title=A Fourier-free proof of the Furstenberg-Sarkozy theorem|work=What's new|first=Terry|last=Tao|authorlink=Terence Tao|date=February 28, 2013}}</ref>  The best upper bound currently known is due to [[Thomas Bloom]] and [[James Maynard (mathematician)|James Maynard]],<ref>{{Cite arXiv|last1=Bloom |first1=Thomas F. |last2=Maynard |first2=James |title=A new upper bound for sets with no square differences |date=24 February 2021|class=math.NT |eprint=2011.13266 }}</ref> who show that a square-difference-free set can include at most
<math display=block>O\!\left(\frac{n}{(\log n)^{c\log\log\log n}} \right)</math>
of the integers from <math>0</math> to <math>n</math>, as expressed in [[big O notation]], where <math>c>0</math> is some absolute constant.

Most of these proofs that establish quantitative upper bounds use [[Fourier analysis]] or [[ergodic theory]], although neither is necessary to prove the weaker result that every square-difference-free set has zero density.<ref name="tao"/>
==Lower bounds==
[[Paul Erdős]] conjectured that every square-difference-free set has
<math display=block>O(n^{1/2}\log^k n)</math>
elements up to <math>n</math>, for some constant <math>k</math>, but this was disproved by Sárközy, who proved that denser sequences exist. Sárközy weakened Erdős's conjecture to suggest that, for every <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, every square-difference-free set has
<math display=block>O(n^{1/2+\varepsilon})</math>
elements up to <math>n</math>.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Sárközy | first = A. | authorlink = András Sárközy
 | journal = Annales Universitatis Scientiarum Budapestinensis de Rolando Eötvös Nominatae
 | mr = 536201
 | pages = 45–53 (1979)
 | title = On difference sets of sequences of integers. II
 | volume = 21
 | year = 1978}}.</ref> This, in turn, was disproved by [[Imre Z. Ruzsa]], who found square-difference-free sets with up to
<math display=block>\Omega\big(n^{(1 \,+\, \log_{65}7)/2}\big) \approx n^{0.733077}</math>
elements.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Ruzsa | first = I. Z. | authorlink = Imre Z. Ruzsa
 | doi = 10.1007/BF02454169
 | issue = 3
 | journal = Periodica Mathematica Hungarica
 | mr = 756185
 | pages = 205–209
 | title = Difference sets without squares
 | volume = 15
 | year = 1984| s2cid = 122624503 }}.</ref>

Ruzsa's construction chooses a [[square-free integer|square-free]] integer <math>b</math> as the [[radix]] of the base-<math>b</math> notation for the integers, such that there exists a large set <math>R</math> of numbers from <math>0</math> to <math>b-1</math> none of whose difference are squares [[modular arithmetic|modulo]] <math>b</math>. He then chooses his square-difference-free set to be the numbers that, in base-<math>b</math> notation, have members of <math>R</math> in their [[parity (mathematics)|even]] digit positions. The digits in [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] positions of these numbers can be arbitrary. Ruzsa found the seven-element set <math>R = \{0,15,21,27,42,48,59\}</math> modulo <math>b=65</math>, giving the stated bound.
Subsequently, Ruzsa's construction has been improved by using a different base, <math>b=205</math>, to give square-difference-free sets with size<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Beigel | first1 = Richard
 | last2 = Gasarch | first2 = William | author2-link = William Gasarch
 | arxiv = 0804.4892
 | title = Square-difference-free sets of size <math>\Omega(n^{0.7334\dots})</math>
 | year = 2008| bibcode = 2008arXiv0804.4892B}}.</ref><ref>{{citation
 | last = Lewko | first = Mark
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Electronic Journal of Combinatorics]]
 | mr = 3315474
 | at = Paper P1.32, 6pp
 | title = An improved lower bound related to the Furstenberg-Sárközy theorem
 | url = http://www.combinatorics.org/ojs/index.php/eljc/article/view/v22i1p32
 | volume = 22
 | year = 2015| article-number = P1.32
 | doi = 10.37236/4656
 | doi-access = free
 }}.</ref>
<math display=block>\Omega\big(n^{(1 \,+\, \log_{205}12)/2}\big) \approx n^{0.733412}.</math>
When applied to the base <math>b=2</math>, the same construction generates the [[Moser–de Bruijn sequence]] multiplied by two, a square-difference-free set of <math>O(n^{1/2})</math> elements. This is too sparse to provide nontrivial lower bounds on the Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem but the same sequence has other notable mathematical properties.<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A000695|name=Moser-de Bruijn sequence|mode=cs2}}</ref>

{{unsolved|mathematics|Is there an exponent <math>c<1</math> such that every square-difference-free subset of <math>[0,n]</math> has <math>O(n^c)</math> elements?}}
Based on these results, it has been conjectured that for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math>
and every sufficiently large <math>n</math> there exist square-difference-free subsets of the numbers from <math>0</math> to <math>n</math> with <math>\Omega(n^{1-\varepsilon})</math> elements. That is, if this conjecture is true, the exponent of one in the upper bounds for the Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem cannot be lowered.<ref name="l13"/>
As an alternative possibility, the exponent 3/4 has been identified as "a natural limitation to Ruzsa's construction" and another candidate for the true maximum growth rate of these sets.<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Lyall | first1 = Neil
 | last2 = Rice | first2 = Alex
 | arxiv = 1504.04904
 | title = Difference sets and polynomials
 | year = 2015| bibcode = 2015arXiv150404904L}}.</ref>

==Generalization to other polynomials==
The upper bound of the Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem can be generalized from sets that avoid square differences to sets that avoid differences in <math>p(\mathbb{N})</math>,
the values at integers of a polynomial <math>p</math> with integer [[coefficient]]s, as long as the values of <math>p</math> include an integer multiple of every integer.
The condition on multiples of integers is necessary for this result, because if there is an integer <math>k</math> whose multiples do not appear in <math>p(\mathbb{N})</math>, then the multiples of <math>k</math> would form a set of nonzero density with no differences in <math>p(\mathbb{N})</math>.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Rice | first = Alex
 | arxiv = 1612.01760
 | doi = 10.4064/aa170828-26-8
 | issue = 1
 | journal = Acta Arithmetica
 | mr = 3884220
 | pages = 1–41
 | title = A maximal extension of the best-known bounds for the Furstenberg–Sárközy theorem
 | volume = 187
 | year = 2019| s2cid = 119139825
 }}</ref>
